questions.explain: The operator is the symbol, +. The values it works on are its operands. An operator produces a new value from them.
/ divides and keeps the decimals, % gives what is left after dividing (7 = 2 × 3 + 1), and ** is power: 2 × 2 × 2.
The remainder keeps the sign of the left side. So -7 % 3 is -1, and 7 % -3 is 1.
questions.code:
console.log(-7 % 3);
console.log(7 % -3);

questions.explain: An even number divided by 2 leaves nothing over, so its remainder is 0. For odd numbers the remainder is 1 (or -1 for negative odd numbers).
a++ gives the old value (1), then adds 1. ++a adds 1 first, then gives the new value (3).

questions.q: How does the lesson tell you to use count++?
questions.explain: a++ and ++a give back different values, which confuses readers. On its own line, both forms simply add 1, so there is nothing to confuse.
options: Inside bigger expressions, like total = count++ * 2, to save a line
On a line of its own, never using its value inside a bigger expression

questions.explain: A compound assignment does the calculation and stores the result in one step. x op= y means x = x op y.
+= also works on strings: it joins the new text to the end. After two joins, the log holds all three parts.

questions.q: What kind of value does a comparison like 5 > 3 always give back?
questions.explain: Comparison operators (>, <, >=, <=, ===, !==) always give true or false.
options: The bigger of the two values

questions.explain: Strings are compared character by character, like words in a dictionary, and "1" comes before "9". Convert text to numbers first to compare them as numbers.

questions.q: What is the difference between === and ==?
questions.explain: Strict equality === never converts. Loose equality == applies coercion first, so "1" == 1 is true while "1" === 1 is false.
options: === is faster, but they always give the same answer
=== needs the same type and value; == first converts the values to a common type

questions.explain: == converts both sides first: "1" becomes 1 and "" becomes 0. === sees a string and a number, so it says false.
== treats null and undefined as equal; === does not, since they are different types. NaN is never equal to anything, not even itself.
questions.code: console.log(null == undefined, null === undefined, NaN === NaN);

questions.q: Which comparison should you write to check that status is the number 0?
questions.explain: Always use ===. status == 0 is also true for "" and false, status = 0 assigns instead of comparing, and !status is true for every falsy value.

questions.q: The lesson allows one common use of ==. Which one?
questions.explain: value == null is true only for null and undefined, which is a useful and safe shortcut. Everywhere else, use ===.
options: value == 0, to check for zero or empty text
value == null, to check for null or undefined in one go
value == true, to check for any truthy value

questions.explain: Both sides of the && are true. Neither side of the || is true. Two nots turn any value into a boolean, and a non-empty string is truthy.
With &&, a falsy left side ends it. With ||, a truthy left side ends it. In both cases the right side is skipped.
options: An error when a condition is too long
&& and || stop as soon as they know the answer, so the right side may never run
Running both sides of && at the same time
Turning any value into a boolean with !!

questions.explain: && and || give back one of their values: the one where they stopped. 0 is falsy, so && stops there and gives 0.
options:
Ada
anonymous
logged in
never checked

questions.explain: The left side of && is false, so JavaScript already knows the answer and never runs the right side.

questions.q: A user picked priority 0 ("lowest"). Why is chosenPriority || 2 a bug?
questions.explain: || replaces every falsy value, including 0 and "", which are often perfectly valid. Use ?? for defaults.
options: 0 is falsy, so || throws the valid choice away and gives 2
It is not a bug; 0 is not a real priority

questions.explain: ?? replaces only nullish values: null and undefined. 0, "" and false are kept.
options: When a is any falsy value, such as 0 or ""

questions.explain: ?? keeps 0 and false, because they are not nullish. Only null and undefined are replaced.
questions.code: console.log(0 ?? 20, false ?? true, null ?? 20, undefined ?? 20);

questions.explain: The empty string is falsy, so || replaces it. It is not nullish, so ?? keeps it, and the brackets show nothing between them.
??= assigns only when the variable is null or undefined. The first line sets 25; the second does nothing, because pageSize is already set.
Optional chaining ?. checks the value on its left. If it is null or undefined, it stops and gives undefined instead of crashing.
Reading .name of null throws a TypeError. With ?. it gives undefined instead, and ?? then supplies the default.

questions.q: Your backend receives request.user, which may be null. Which line reads the user's name safely, with "guest" as the default?
questions.explain: ?. avoids the crash when user is null, and ?? supplies the default only when the name is really missing. Without ?., reading .name of null throws.
+ runs left to right. Once a string appears, every later + joins text. In the last line the numbers are added first (3), and only then joined with the text.
&& binds tighter than ||, so the first line is true || (false && false), which is true. Parentheses change the order in the second line.
questions.code:
console.log(true || false && false);
console.log((true || false) && false);

questions.explain: ! runs before ===, so it flips a first. If you mean "a is not equal to b", write a !== b.

questions.q: Which of these is a syntax error in JavaScript?
questions.explain: JavaScript refuses to guess whether -2 ** 2 means (-2) ** 2 or -(2 ** 2), so it is a syntax error. Add parentheses to say which you mean.

questions.q: You write a || b ?? c. What happens?
questions.explain: Mixing ?? with || or && without parentheses is not allowed. Add parentheses to make the order clear.
options: It is a syntax error: mixing ?? with || needs parentheses

questions.q: You are not sure which operator in a long expression runs first. What does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: Parentheses remove the doubt, for you and for the next reader. You do not need to memorise the whole table.
options: Learn the full precedence table by heart
Split the expression over several lines without changing it
Add parentheses: they cost nothing and make the order obvious

questions.explain: minStock 0 and the empty search were sent on purpose, and ?? keeps them. Only the missing user name gets its default. With ||, minStock would be 5 and search *.

questions.q: Finish isEven so it returns true for even numbers and false for odd ones. Use % and ===.
questions.explain: An even number leaves no remainder when divided by 2: n % 2 === 0. The comparison already gives a boolean, so return it directly.

questions.q: Fix the default: the program should print Volume: 0 for the user who turned the volume all the way down, and Volume: 50 only when there is no setting.
questions.explain: || threw away the valid 0, because 0 is falsy. ?? replaces only null and undefined.

questions.q: Finish cityOf so it returns the city of the order's customer address, or "unknown" when any part is missing. It must not crash. The program should print Lagos and then unknown twice.
questions.explain: Put ?. after every part that may be missing, so reading stops with undefined instead of crashing. Then ?? "unknown" supplies the default.

questions.q: Finish formatDuration so it turns minutes into hours and minutes: formatDuration(135) returns "2h 15m". Use Math.floor for the whole hours and % for the minutes left over.
questions.explain: Math.floor(minutes / 60) gives the whole hours and minutes % 60 the minutes left over. A template literal joins them.

questions.q: This prints Total: 12 instead of Total: 3. Fix it so it prints Total: 3.
questions.explain: The first + makes a string, and every + after it joins text. Put the sum in parentheses so it is calculated first.

questions.q: Finish canEdit: a user can edit a task when they are the task's owner and the task is not done, or when they are an admin. Use ===, &&, || and !, with parentheses. The program should print true false true false.
questions.explain: (user.name === task.owner && !task.done) || user.isAdmin === true. The parentheses are not strictly needed, since && binds tighter, but they make the rule obvious to the reader.

questions.q: Finish readFilters: read minStock (default 5) and pageSize (default 20) from query, which may be missing. A minStock of 0 ("show sold-out products too") is sent on purpose and must be kept. Return the text minStock=… size=….
questions.explain: query?.minStock avoids the crash when query is missing, and ?? keeps the 0. With ||, a minStock of 0 would wrongly become 5.
questions.expected:
minStock=0 size=20
minStock=3 size=10
minStock=5 size=20

questions.q: Finish isZero so it returns true only for the number 0. The empty string and false must give false. The program should print true false false false.
questions.explain: value === 0 needs the same type and value. value == 0 would also be true for "", false and "0", because == converts them first.

questions.q: Start score at 10. Using only compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=), add 5, then take away 3, then double it, and print the result after each step: 15, 12, 24.
questions.explain: score += 5 is short for score = score + 5. The same pattern works for -= and *=.

questions.q: Finish fillDefaults with ??=: give config.port the default 3000 and config.host the default "localhost", but only when they are missing. A port of 0 sent on purpose must stay 0.
questions.explain: x ??= value assigns only when x is null or undefined. ||= would replace the valid port 0 with 3000.
order.x === undefined cannot tell a property that holds undefined from a property that does not exist: both lines say true. in asks whether the property exists, so it tells them apart.
1 | 4 switches on bits 001 and 100, which is 101, or 5. 5 & 2 is 0 because the EDIT bit is off, so the test is false. Adding EDIT gives 111, and toString(2) prints it in binary.
typeof is a unary operator, and unary operators run before +. So it is (typeof 1) + 2: the string "number" joined with 2. To get the type of the sum, write typeof (1 + 2).

questions.q: Old code drops the decimals of an amount in kobo with amount | 0. Why should you replace it with Math.trunc(amount)?
questions.explain: Every bitwise operator first converts its operands to 32-bit integers. 7.9 | 0 is 7, as intended, but 3000000000 | 0 is -1294967296. Math.trunc works on every number.
options: Bitwise operators convert to a 32-bit whole number, so amounts above about 2.1 billion (₦21 million in kobo) wrap around to wrong, even negative, values
| 0 rounds to the nearest whole number instead of cutting off the decimals
| 0 turns the amount into a string
There is no difference; it is only a matter of style
